newsitem.title: FRANCE: Le Pen says Front is France's only real opposition.
newsitem.headline: Le Pen says Front is France's only real opposition.

text.p: Far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said on Wednesday that his National Front's sole parliamentarian was the true opposition to the new leftist majority in France and he urged disillusioned rightists to join his ranks.
"The National Front is truly the only genuine opposition to the Socialo-Communist Left," the fiery Le Pen told a news conference at party headquarters.

"We will be the core of a national, popular and social opposition," he said, inviting supporters of the squabbling outgoing centre-right majority to join forces with him in a major regrouping of the French right.

Just one National Front candidate, Toulon Mayor Jean-Marie Le Chevallier, triumphed in Sunday's parliamentary election in which a leftist alliance including Communists and Socialists snatched power from a centre-right coalition.
Le Pen said Le Chevallier would be the Front's "loyal spokesman" in the leftist-dominated National Assembly and serve as a base for the party's future growth there.
Le Pen, 68, said the role would not diminish his own standing as party leader.

He said the party would try to harness the "enormous forces" of disappointed voters of the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) and the Union for French Democracy (UDF), the two main components of the defeated coalition.
Both are scrambling to place blame for Sunday's defeat.
"While waiting (for them to join us), we will keep up our propaganda, organisational, grassroots and training efforts as well as efforts to spread our ideas," Le Pen said.
The National Front won a hefty 14.94 percent of the first-round vote in the parliamentary election, compared to 12.4 percent in the last parliamentary vote in 1993.

It was able to place its candidates in 132 of France's 577 constituencies in last Sunday's runoff vote, a figure widely seen by analysts as a sign that the Front was now a major force in all French elections.
But just one of those candidates went on to win an assembly seat, and Le Pen said party officials would meet on June 14 to begin preparing a strategy for approaching regional and local elections.
Le Pen flatly rejected suggestions that his own conduct might have hurt his party's cause.

During the campaign's final two days, the hefty former paratrooper threw a female Socialist candidate to the ground, shouted obscenities at protesters and paraded around the stage at a Paris rally carrying an oversized photograph of the head of Socialist candidate Catherine Trautmann on a platter.
Asked about his behaviour on those occasions, he said he "deeply regretted" Trautmann's victory in her eastern constituency.
"She barely escaped the voters' guillotine," Le Pen said.
Trautmann recently led an anti-Front protest in the eastern city of Strasbourg, where she is mayor.
